title: ElkShore throughput & latency characterization call
summary: First discovery focused on p95 latency and throughput needs for ElkShore's real-time summarization product. Customer is weighing Redwood hosted for speed of onboarding vs Dedicated/Private for data residency and consistent p95. Agreed to run a short token/sec benchmark and follow up with dedicated sizing worksheet and security docs.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-08-13
Time: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees: Alice Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Sanjay Patel (CTO - ElkShore), Maya Li (Lead ML Eng), Owen R. (Infra)

Auto-summary: Quick discovery to map p95 targets and throughput for a streaming summarization use-case. Heavy focus on p95 at tail, fallback policies, and whether hosted can meet SLOs or if they need Dedicated/Private for predictable tail latency and KMS integration.

[00:00] Alice Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um, on today's agenda we want to understand your latency SLOs, concurrency patterns, and what kind of streaming or token/sec behavior you have. Sanjay, do you want to kick off with a little context?

[00:17] Sanjay Patel: Sure, yep, thanks Alice. So ElkShore runs a real-time meeting summarization product embedded in our web client. Typical sessions are 10 to 60 minutes, but we do incremental summaries every 5-10 seconds of new transcript. So it's very streaming-y, like token bursts. Our SLA is customer-facing: p95 end-to-end summary update under 250 ms ideally, but we know that includes network and client processing. The core ask is can Redwood meet p95 generation under 120-150 ms at our expected concurrency.

[00:48] Marco Ruiz: Quick clarification — is the 120-150 ms target purely for server gen time (inference) or end-to-end?

[00:53] Maya Li: It's really server-side. We instrumented our current stack, and network/client takes roughly 80 to 100 ms, so we want inference not to blow out the p95.

[01:10] Alice Chen: Got it. And volume-wise, what's peak concurrent requests per region?

[01:15] Maya Li: Peak concurrency is about 600 concurrent users in US-East during lunch hour, each producing a burst of short prompts every 5-8s. Average tokens per prompt is 30, average tokens generated ~60. So tokens/sec is spiky — like short bursts of 3k to 6k tokens/sec sustained over a few seconds.

[01:40] Owen R.: And the customer data is PII, so we'll need encryption at rest and KMS integration, also SOC2 and audit logs; may need a private deployment if we can't get those guarantees in hosted.

[01:52] Marco Ruiz: Understood. So couple of axes: latency SLO at p95, steady-state throughput, and cold start/kind of KV cache behavior for streaming with KV cache/prefix caching. For streaming, we can keep KV cache warm for a session, which really helps tail for incremental tokens.

[02:10] Sanjay Patel: Can you explain the KV cache bit more? We've seen people talk about KV cache but not sure how it translates to our per-session summaries.

[02:18] Marco Ruiz: Yeah. So when you do iterative summaries of a conversation, the model keeps a KV cache of previous context so subsequent tokens don't need to recompute full attention on the full prefix. That reduces per-token latency as session grows. On Redwood hosted, we have session affinity options and prefix caching to keep that state cached in memory; on Dedicated we can pin sessions to GPUs for even lower tail latency. On Private you manage the cache, so it's super predictable but needs ops work.

[02:50] Maya Li: Do you have numbers for how much p95 drops with warm KV cache vs cold?

[02:55] Marco Ruiz: Ballpark: warm token latency can be 20-40% lower than cold for the same model and batch size, because we avoid recomputing prefix. But it depends on seqlen and model architecture. We'll need to measure with your prompt distribution.

[03:09] Sanjay Patel: Ok. Another question: how do you handle batching for short prompts? Batching helps throughput but hurts latency.

[03:15] Alice Chen: Right, so our runtime does continuous batching and you can configure latency SLOs so the router will trade off batching vs single-request latency. For strict p95 we can set a tight latency budget and the router will prioritise immediate dispatch to avoid waiting for batch fill. That means higher cost per token but lower tail.

[03:33] Owen R.: If we go Dedicated, do we get stricter controls over batching thresholds?

[03:36] Marco Ruiz: Yes, Dedicated gives you more control — and you can size GPU pools to match concurrency so batching behavior becomes predictable. Also Dedicated supports reserving warm pools and pre-warmed models which reduces cold starts.

[03:49] Maya Li: We also want to minimize jitter at p95 across multi-region. We plan to route users to us-east primarily, with failover to us-west. How's multi-region routing handled?

[03:59] Alice Chen: We support region routing by policy, and you can configure fallback policies. For strict p95 we usually recommend keeping active capacity in your primary region and a readied failover in secondaries. If you need guaranteed cross-region p95, Dedicated or Private with multi-region deployment is safer. Hosted can do it but there's more variability during spikes.

[04:27] Sanjay Patel: What about model choice — are you suggesting a smaller model for latency? We're currently on an in-house tuned LLaMA-ish variant but might consider Redwood-curated models.

[04:36] Marco Ruiz: Model choice matters a lot — smaller, int8/4-bit quantized models reduce per-token latency. Redwood Optimize can recommend quant profiles. There's a tradeoff between quality and latency; for short summary updates you might tolerate a smaller decoder and then run a higher-quality recap less frequently.

[04:56] Maya Li: Hmm might be an interesting hybrid: low-latency incremental summaries with a high-quality batch recap every minute. That could reduce overall cost and p95 pressure.

[05:05] Owen R.: On Private, can we integrate our HSM/KMS for key management? We need envelope encryption keys in our HSM.

[05:12] Alice Chen: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations. Dedicated supports KMS integrations too but for HSM-level custody we recommend Private. We'll share the KMS integration doc.

[05:26] Sanjay Patel: Let's talk numbers — can Redwood hit 120-150ms server-side p95 for token generation for ~600 concurrency with those short token bursts?

[05:36] Marco Ruiz: Short answer: probably not on hosted at scale without specialized tuning and warm pools; hosted may hit it for lighter loads but for 600 concurrent bursty sessions Dedicated with pinned warm pools or Private are much more predictable. But we should run a benchmark. Proposed test: we spin up a dedicated bench harness simulating 600 concurrent sessions, average prompt 30 tokens, generate 60 tokens, repeat bursts every 6s for a 10-minute window and measure p50/p95/p99.

[06:03] Maya Li: That sounds good. What hardware do you plan to run on? We have cost limits and want a realistic estimate for GS/RTX class.

[06:11] Marco Ruiz: For initial profiling we suggest testing on a few instance types — e.g., A100-class and an accelerated inference config (like 80GB and quantized 8-bit on cost-optimized Ampere). For Dedicated we can propose a mix. We'll include Redwood's performance profiles per model+hardware so you can see tokens/sec and p95 numbers.

[06:37] Sanjay Patel: For the benchmark, can we also see impact of batch sizes and router latency budgets — like run three runs: aggressive batching, balanced, and low-latency mode?

[06:46] Alice Chen: Absolutely. We'll run multi-config tests and provide the CSV with p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.

[06:52] Owen R.: One more infra question — do you manage GPU preemption or eviction? If a node is evicted, how graceful is fallover for in-flight streaming sessions?

[07:02] Marco Ruiz: For Dedicated and Private we have controlled eviction policies — Dedicated has SLA-backed capacity so evictions are rare. The runtime supports graceful fallback: we checkpoint KV cache periodically and have automatic retries to a fallback model variant in another pool. For hosted we have multi-tenant constraints and fallbacks to smaller model variants if capacity is constrained. We can show our fallback policy diagram.

[07:25] Sanjay Patel: Sounds good. Any compliance gaps we should be worried about?

[07:30] Alice Chen: We are SOC2 Type II, and we can provide detailed audit/logging for Dedicated and Private. Hosted includes audit logs but for some audit requirements customers want Private to own the logs. We'll attach the security pack.

[07:43] Maya Li: On telemetry — we need token-level latency traces. Does Redwood expose per-token latency or just per-request?

[07:49] Marco Ruiz: We expose detailed token-level traces in Redwood Console for Dedicated and can push traces to your tracing backend via traces hooks. Hosted exposes summarized metrics but we can enable more detailed debug traces during benchmark windows.

[08:05] Sanjay Patel: Ok next let's lock down the benchmark window. We want to minimize user disruption but need realistic load. Owen, can your infra team give a couple of windows next week?

[08:14] Owen R.: Yes, I'll ping ops and propose Thu/Fri next week mornings. I'll share a calendar invite after.

[08:20] Alice Chen: Great. We'll draft the harness and send it to Marco and Owen for sign-off.

[08:25] Maya Li: Slight tangent — cost sensitivity. If we go low-latency mode with tight latency budgets and low batching, cost per token may spike. Can you provide rough cost tradeoff numbers?

[08:35] Marco Ruiz: We'll include a cost-vs-latency spreadsheet — two axes: cost per 1k tokens vs achieved p95 for each model/hardware/config. Historically, reducing batching to hit sub-150ms p95 increases cost 1.8-2.3x compared to optimized batching. We'll provide more precise estimates after the benchmark.

[08:56] Sanjay Patel: Also want to know runbook for on-call when p95 spikes. How do fallbacks and alerts work?

[09:04] Alice Chen: Redwood Console supports per-route SLO alerts, and you can configure automatic fallback to a lower-cost model or different region. We'll demo the runbook and escalation paths in the next call.

[09:18] Marco Ruiz: Quick note on quantization — some of the earlier generation quant tools can change output distribution; we recommend running quality regressions tied to your prompt set. Redwood Optimize can automate those evals and tie them to rollout policies.

[09:35] Maya Li: Ok that is helpful. Any blockers for starting a pilot?

[09:38] Alice Chen: Only thing we need from you is the prompt set and permission to run a 10-20 minute benchmark. We'll use a separate bench account and neutral data handling, then delete logs as per your retention policy.

[09:50] Sanjay Patel: Sounds good. Could you also include a sketch of expected Dedicated sizing for 600 users targeting 150ms p95? Even a rough ballpark will help justify to finance.

[09:58] Marco Ruiz: We'll include a sizing sketch — likely a mix of several GPU nodes with pre-warmed pools; we'll put ranges. We'll be explicit about assumptions (prompt length, model, quant).

[10:12] Owen R.: Final question — any differences in error budgets when streaming partial tokens vs full response streaming? We sometimes send partial deltas to client.

[10:22] Marco Ruiz: Partial streaming increases surface area for transient errors — but our streaming runtime supports resumable streams and tokenized ACKs so the client can re-request missing token ranges. This is more robust in Dedicated/Private where session affinity is guaranteed.

[10:40] Alice Chen: Ok, we've got good alignment. Recap of next steps: Alice shares pricing & security docs; Marco shares benchmark harness and coordinate runs with Owen; Maya shares prompt set; Owen schedules infra window.

[10:55] Sanjay Patel: Appreciate the time. If the benchmark looks good, we'll likely pilot Dedicated capacity for the US-East region and consider Private for EU data residency.

[11:05] Alice Chen: Perfect. We'll follow up with an email thread and get the invites on the calendar. Thanks everyone.

[11:12] -- end meeting --

Notes on transcript quality: intermittent mis-attribution of speakers in the live notes, a few filler words, some technical acronyms may be slightly garbled (e.g., HSM spelled out or heard as H S M).
